                 Abstract
                 Japan is advancing carbon dioxide capture and storage (CCS) initiatives to achieve carbon neutrality by
                 2050, identifying depleted oil and gas fields as promising storage sites. Among these, the Higashi-Niigata
                 gas field – known for its long production history and extensive subsurface data — has been selected as a
                 candidate site under the Advanced CCS Projects program led by the Japan Organization for Metals and
                 Energy Security (JOGMEC).
                    Due to Japan's unique geological conditions, storage reservoirs are not always as favorable as those
                 found in other countries. However, the Higashi-Niigata field, being a depleted gas field with a long
                 production history and abundant data, offers a distinct advantage over data-scarce aquifers for precise
                 storage planning. In this study, Japan Petroleum Exploration Co., Ltd. (JAPEX) and MITSUBISHI GAS
                 CHEMICAL COMPANY, INC.(MGC) jointly conducted a comprehensive reservoir evaluation to assess the
                 feasibility of CCS implementation at the Higashi-Niigata field. Before initiating a reservoir evaluation, the
                 seal integrity and fault stability were evaluated using geological and production history data. A geological
                 model was constructed, and a reservoir simulation model was developed through history matching, despite
                 the complexity of the interbedded sand and mud formations characteristic of the field.
                    By leveraging extensive subsurface data and incorporating multiple geological realizations calibrated
                 through history matching, the study achieved a highly accurate CO2 storage plan. This plan enabled the
                 quantitative assessment of injection performance, pressure evolution, and storage capacity. The inclusion
                 of case studies involving pressure relief wells further highlighted optimization strategies for preserving
                 reservoir integrity and enhancing storage potential.
                    The study demonstrated that the Higashi-Niigata gas field is a suitable and strategic candidate for CCS
                 in Japan, with reliable injectivity, capacity, and integrity confirmed through simulation and data analysis.

                    In this context, Japan Petroleum Exploration Co., Ltd. (JAPEX) is planning CCS and carbon dioxide
                 capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) projects to contribute to Japan's overall CO2 reduction target of
                 approximately 760 million tons. The Higashi-Niigata region, located along the Japan Sea, is one of Japan's
                 major oil and gas production hubs and is surrounded by a concentration of CO2 emission sources such
                 as thermal power plants and chemical factories, with total annual emissions estimated at several million
                 tons. Leveraging these geographical and industrial characteristics, a ‘hub-and-cluster’ CCS project is being
                 conceptualized in this region, in which CO2 collected from multiple emitters is aggregated via pipelines and
                 injected underground for storage.
                    This paper reports on the results of a reservoir study promoted by a five-company consortium, including
                 JAPEX, as part of the Higashi-Niigata CCS project selected by JOGMEC in 2024 as one of the Advanced
                 CCS Projects.

                 Technical workflow
                 Overview of the Target
                 Japan Petroleum Exploration Co., Ltd. (JAPEX) and MITSUBISHI GAS CHEMICAL COMPANY, INC.
                 (MGC) discovered the Higashi-Niigata gas field, located in Niigata Prefecture along the Japan Sea coast,
                 in 1959. Over 40 wells have been drilled in this field. After approximately 50 years of development and
                 production, the field is now in a late-mature stage.
                    In recent years, gas and oil production have declined due to pressure depletion and water production,
                 prompting growing interest in the potential for CO2 injection into depleted reservoirs.
                    The Higashi-Niigata field comprises multiple reservoirs, each overlain by independent seal formations.
                 One of these multiple reservoirs has the highest cumulative production volumes, and this reservoir is
                 considered a promising candidate for CO2 storage.

                 CO2 Storage Suitability in the Field
                 This section summarizes the CO2 storage suitability of the Higashi-Niigata gas field from the perspectives
                 of the reservoir, seal, and fault.
                 Reservoir. Among the multiple candidate formations, one was selected as the primary storage target, while
                 the others were evaluated as secondary candidates. These formations are in a supercritical condition and
                 exhibit favorable horizontal continuity and pressure communication, suggesting their suitability for CO2
                 storage. The reservoir simulations described later were conducted with the primary objective of confirming
                 these characteristics.
                 Seal. Immediately above the target reservoirs lies a mudstone seal formation with a thickness of
                 50–120 meters, which has historically retained hydrocarbons, indicating strong sealing capacity for
                 CO2. Additionally, multiple overlying production layers may act as secondary or tertiary seals, thereby
                 minimizing the risk of surface leakage.

                 Faults. Seismic data and existing well information indicate the presence of multiple faults within the field.
                 However, based on production data and observed fluid composition changes, the faults separating different
                 reservoirs are interpreted to have low transmissibility. Therefore, the risk of CO2 migration through faults
                 is considered low if injection is conducted into the targeted reservoir formation.
                    Based on these findings, the reservoir exhibiting the most favorable properties within the Higashi-Niigata
                 gas field was selected as the primary storage target, and reservoir simulations were subsequently conducted.

                    To address geological uncertainty, 100 realizations were generated by varying key reservoir properties
                 as follows:

                           • Volume of shale (Vsh): Spatial distribution estimated using geostatistical methods based on
                             existing well data.
                           • Porosity: Derived using correlations with Vsh
                           • Permeability: Set using core-based porosity–permeability relationships and Flow Zone Indicator.
                    Subsequently, history matching was performed across all realizations. Based on the results, 10
                 realizations exhibiting good agreement with historical production data were selected for subsequent
                 forecasting analyses.

                 Case A: CO2 Injection with 3 injectors
                 In the initial case, the CO2 injection volume was evaluated by operating three injection wells. The placement
                 of the injection wells is shown in Figure 10. It was designed to balance two objectives: (1) promoting
                 residual trapping and dissolution by positioning wells deeper, and (2) minimizing deliverability uncertainty
                 by situating wells closer to the central area, where extensive geological and production data are available.
                 The results are presented in Figure 11 and 12.

                 Case B: CO2 Injection with Pressure Relief Wells
                 Since the evaluation was conducted using a reservoir model, a case incorporating pressure relief wells was
                 examined as an option to secure greater storage capacity by incorporating water production into the material
                 balance framework.
                    The locations of the injection wells and pressure relief wells are shown in Figure 16. The results are
                 presented in Figure 17 and Figure 18. The placement of the pressure relief wells was also designed to balance
                 two objectives: (1) distancing them from the injection wells to mitigate CO2 breakthrough, and (2) situating
                 them closer to the central area, where extensive geological and production data reduce deliverability
                 uncertainty.

                           • It was observed that the CO2 injection volume increased by approximately 25% to 30% compared
                             to Case A.
                           • The time at which the reservoir pressure reached the upper threshold was delayed compared to
                             Case A, confirming the effectiveness of the pressure relief wells (Figure 19).

                 Conclusion
                 This study assessed the CCS technical feasibility in the Higashi-Niigata gas field, a depleted gas reservoir
                 in Japan. A comprehensive geological evaluation, reservoir modeling, and simulation study were conducted
                 to characterize the CO2 storage potential and the injection behavior under various operational scenarios.
                    Leveraging the extensive subsurface data available from this mature gas field, the reservoir simulation
                 study enabled the construction of a highly accurate CO2 storage plan. By incorporating multiple geological
                 realizations and conducting history matching, the study quantitatively assessed injection performance,
                 pressure behavior, and storage capacity under various operational conditions. This methodology helped
                 reduce the uncertainties typically associated with CCS projects in undeveloped formations and demonstrated
                 the viability of site-specific, detailed storage planning. Case studies, including the scenarios utilizing
                 pressure relief wells, offered valuable insights for optimizing injection operations while preserving reservoir
                 integrity.
                    Given its long production history, extensive subsurface data, and comprehensive reservoir studies, the
                 Higashi-Niigata field demonstrates not only high technical feasibility for CCS implementation but also
                 significant potential as a strategic CCS hub within the "hub-and-cluster" framework promoted in Japan.
                 These findings are expected to contribute to the establishment of large-scale CCS infrastructure and the
                 achievement of national carbon neutrality targets.
